hmmt-nov-2009-guts-01.title: Reciprocals
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-01.body:
Since $\frac1{f(x)}=1+\frac1x$, each application of $f$ adds $1$ to the reciprocal. After four applications $\frac1{f^4(x)}=\frac1x+4=\frac{1+4x}{x}$, so $f^4(2009)=\frac{2009}{8037}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2009}{8037}$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-02.title: Colouring and reachability
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-02.body:
A knight changes square colour on every move, so after an odd number of moves it must be on a square of the colour opposite to the starting one: at most $32$ squares.

Every such square can be reached. The knight's graph on the board is connected, and any square is within $6$ moves of the corner, so each opposite-coloured square is reachable in some odd number $m\le 6$ of moves. The remaining $2009-m$ moves (an even number) can be spent moving to a neighbouring square and back. Hence all $32$ squares of the opposite colour can be reached.

**Answer: 32**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-03.title: Geometric series
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-03.body:
Each inscribed circle has diameter equal to the side of the square around it, and the next square inscribed in that circle has diagonal equal to that diameter, so its area is half of the previous square. The squares have areas $1,\frac12,\frac14,\dots$ with sum $2$. Each circle has area $\frac\pi4$ times the area of the square around it, so the circles sum to $2\cdot\frac\pi4=\frac\pi2$. The difference is $2-\frac\pi2$.

**Answer: $2-\frac{\pi}{2}$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-04.title: Count the diagonals
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-04.body:
There are $12$ face diagonals (two on each of the $6$ faces), each of length $\sqrt2$, and $4$ space diagonals of length $\sqrt3$. The product is $(\sqrt2)^{12}(\sqrt3)^4=64\cdot9=576$.

**Answer: 576**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-05.title: Symmetry
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-05.body:
After the first card is thrown, $9$ cards remain, and the last card thrown is equally likely to be any of them. Exactly $4$ of those have the same colour as the first card. Probability $\frac49$.

**Answer: $\frac49$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-06.title: Work mod 100
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-06.body:
$1032^{1032}\equiv32^{1032}\pmod{100}$. The last two digits of $32^k$ for $k=1,2,3,4,5$ are $32,24,68,76,32$, so they repeat with period $4$. Since $1032\equiv0\pmod 4$, the last two digits are those of $32^4$, namely $76$.

**Answer: 76**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-07.title: Count functions
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-07.body:
There are $2^4=16$ possible inputs, and each can be assigned one of $2$ outputs independently, giving $2^{16}=65536$ functions.

**Answer: 65536**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-08.title: Exterior angles
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-08.body:
The exterior angles ($180^\circ$ minus each interior angle) also form an arithmetic progression with common difference $d=\pm$ (an integer, nonzero); order them so $d\ge1$ is positive, with smallest term $x>0$. They sum to $360^\circ$:
$$nx+\frac{n(n-1)}2d=360.$$
Since $nx>0$ and $d\ge1$, we get $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}<360$, i.e. $n(n-1)<720$, so $n\le27$ ($27\cdot26=702$, $28\cdot27=756$).

$n=27$ works: take $d=1$, $x=\frac{360-351}{27}=\frac13>0$. The exterior angles $\frac13,\frac43,\dots,\frac{79}{3}$ are all positive and less than $180^\circ$, giving a valid convex polygon.

**Answer: 27**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-09.title: Digit sums by hundreds
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-09.body:
Let $f(x)$ be the total digit sum of $0,1,\dots,x$. For $0$ to $99$: each of the $10$ tens digits appears $10$ times, and the same for units digits, so $f(99)=10\cdot45+10\cdot45=900$.

For the block $100a,\dots,100a+99$ (with $a\le 9$), every number has extra leading digit $a$, so the block's digit sum is $100a+900$. Hence $f(100a+99)=\sum_{j=0}^{a}(100j+900)=50a(a+1)+900(a+1)$.

Setting this equal to $10000$: $50a^2+950a-9100=0$, i.e. $a^2+19a-182=0$, $(a+26)(a-7)=0$, so $a=7$. Thus $f(799)=10000$, and $n=799$.

**Answer: 799**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-10.title: Only constant messages
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-10.body:
If the message has at least two distinct letters, the chance that a random rearrangement equals the original is at most $\frac{1}{5}$ (the best case is a message like $aaaab$, where $4!/5!=\frac15$). So the message must be a single letter repeated five times, which survives with probability $1$. There are $26$ such messages.

**Answer: 26**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-11.title: Area model
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-11.body:
The pair of numbers $(x,y)$ is uniformly distributed in the square $[-1,1]^2$ of area $4$. Sarah wins when $x^2+y^2<1$, the unit disc of area $\pi$. Probability $\frac\pi4$.

**Answer: $\frac\pi4$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-12.title: Right triangle
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-12.body:
Triangle $OBC$ has a right angle at $C$ and $\angle BOC=\angle AOB=60^\circ$, so $OC=OB\cos60^\circ=\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-13.title: Pair one at a time
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-13.body:
The first student has $7$ possible partners; of the remaining $6$, a chosen student has $5$ partners; then $3$; then the last two are paired. $7\cdot5\cdot3\cdot1=105$.

**Answer: 105**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-13.title: Order the pairs
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-13.body:
Line up the $8$ students in $8!$ ways and pair consecutive students. Each pairing is counted $4!$ times for the order of the pairs and $2^4$ times for the order inside each pair: $\frac{8!}{4!\,2^4}=105$.

**Answer: 105**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-14.title: Evaluate at 1
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-14.body:
Write $f(x)=(x+x_1)(x+x_2)(x+x_3)(x+x_4)$ with positive integers $x_i$. Then $f(1)=1+a+b+c+d=2010=(1+x_1)(1+x_2)(1+x_3)(1+x_4)$. Since $2010=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot67$ and each factor $1+x_i\ge2$, the factors are exactly $2,3,5,67$, so the $x_i$ are $1,2,4,66$. Then $d=x_1x_2x_3x_4=1\cdot2\cdot4\cdot66=528$.

**Answer: 528**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-15.title: Eliminate x
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-15.body:
Substituting $x^2=y+7$ into the circle: $y^2+y+7=36$, i.e. $y^2+y-29=0$. Its roots $y_1,y_2$ have sum $-1$, and both give $x^2=y+7>0$ (the roots are about $4.9$ and $-5.9$), so each gives two intersection points $x=\pm\sqrt{y+7}$. The sum of $x^2$ over the four points is $2\big((y_1+7)+(y_2+7)\big)=2(-1+14)=26$.

**Answer: 26**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-16.title: Repeating decimal
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-16.body:
$\frac1{99999}=0.\overline{00001}$, with period $00001$ containing $4$ zeros among $5$ digits. The probability is $\frac45$.

**Answer: $\frac45$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-17.title: Distance from center to line
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-17.body:
The center lies on the perpendicular bisector $x=3$ of the chord, so it is $(3,y)$ with radius $r=\sqrt{1+y^2}$. Tangency to $y=x$ means the distance to the line equals $r$: $\frac{|3-y|}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt{1+y^2}$. Squaring: $(3-y)^2=2+2y^2$, so $y^2+6y-7=0$, giving $y=1$ or $y=-7$. The sum is $-6$ (also directly from Vieta).

**Answer: $-6$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-18.title: Linear in each variable
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-18.body:
The first equation says $f(a+1,b,c)-f(a,b,c)=f(a,b,c)-f(a-1,b,c)$, i.e. along each line parallel to an axis $f$ is an arithmetic progression, so it is determined by its values at two consecutive points. Applying this in turn to the $a$, $b$ and $c$ directions, $f$ is determined everywhere by its values at the $8$ points of $\{0,1\}^3$.

Conversely, the $8$ values at these points can be chosen freely: $f(a,b,c)$ equal to any multilinear polynomial $\alpha_0+\alpha_1a+\dots+\alpha_7abc$ satisfies all three conditions, and the $8$ coefficients $\alpha_i$ can be matched to any $8$ values on $\{0,1\}^3$. So fewer than $8$ evaluations cannot determine $f$.

**Answer: 8**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-19.title: Orderings of cuts
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-19.body:
Ignoring the final attack, we order the $8$ cuts (six legs, two claws). The first three cuts must be legs, so the claws sit among the last $5$ cuts. Choose which $2$ of the last $5$ positions are claws: $\binom52=10$ ways; arrange the claws in those positions in $2!$ ways and the legs in the remaining positions in $6!$ ways. Total $6!\cdot2!\cdot\binom52=720\cdot2\cdot10=14400$.

**Answer: 14400**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-20.title: Square plus three triangles
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-20.body:
Centre the circle at the origin. Take the triangle with vertices $(0,1)$ and $(\pm\frac{\sqrt3}2,-\frac12)$ (base horizontal) and the square with vertices $(\pm\frac{\sqrt2}2,\pm\frac{\sqrt2}2)$ (sides parallel to the axes). The heptagon consists of the square (area $2$) and three triangles built on three of its sides:

- On the top side, apex $(0,1)$: base $\sqrt2$, height $1-\frac{\sqrt2}2$, area $\frac12\sqrt2\left(1-\frac{\sqrt2}2\right)=\frac{\sqrt2-1}2$.
- On the left side, apex $(-\frac{\sqrt3}2,-\frac12)$: base $\sqrt2$, height $\frac{\sqrt3-\sqrt2}2$, area $\frac{\sqrt2(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)}4=\frac{\sqrt6-2}4$; the right side is the same.

The bottom side of the square is a side of the heptagon. Total: $2+\frac{\sqrt2-1}2+2\cdot\frac{\sqrt6-2}4=\frac{1+\sqrt2+\sqrt6}2\approx2.43$.

**Answer: $\frac{1+\sqrt2+\sqrt6}2$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-21.title: Track the second coefficient
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-21.body:
$f(x)=(x+1)^2$. If $P(x)=x^n+cx^{n-1}+\cdots$, then $f(P(x))=(P(x)+1)^2=x^{2n}+2c\,x^{2n-1}+\cdots$. So each application of $f$ doubles the degree and doubles the coefficient of the second-highest term. Starting with $f(x)=x^2+2x+1$ (coefficient $2$), after $2009$ applications the coefficient is $2^{2009}$.

**Answer: $2^{2009}$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-22.title: Adjacent swaps only
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-22.body:
Each card either stays or swaps with a neighbour, and swaps must be disjoint adjacent pairs. Count sets of disjoint adjacent pairs among the $4$ adjacent pairs of positions: none: $1$; one pair: $4$; two disjoint pairs: $3$ (pairs $\{1,2\}\{3,4\}$, $\{1,2\}\{4,5\}$, $\{2,3\}\{4,5\}$). Total $1+4+3=8$.

**Answer: 8**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-22.title: Recurrence
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-22.body:
Let $a_n$ be the number of such arrangements of $n$ cards. The last card either stays ($a_{n-1}$) or swaps with the one before it ($a_{n-2}$), so $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$ with $a_1=1,a_2=2$: $1,2,3,5,8$. So $a_5=8$.

**Answer: 8**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-23.title: Telescoping
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-23.body:
Since $a_n=a_{n+2}-a_{n+1}$, $\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}a_{n+2}}=\frac1{a_{n+1}}-\frac1{a_{n+2}}$. The sum telescopes to $\frac1{a_1}-\frac1{a_{10}}$. The sequence is $3,2,5,7,12,19,31,50,81,131,212$, so $a_{10}=212$ and the sum is $\frac12-\frac1{212}=\frac{105}{212}$.

**Answer: $\frac{105}{212}$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-24.title: Cut off corners
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-24.body:
Label the top face $ABCD$ and the bottom face $EFGH$ with $E,F,G,H$ below $A,B,C,D$. Choose $A,B,C,F,H$. The cube minus the hull consists of three corner tetrahedra $CFGH$, $AEFH$, $ACDH$, each with volume $\frac13\cdot\frac12\cdot1=\frac16$. So the hull has volume $1-\frac12=\frac12$.

A computer check over all $\binom85=56$ choices of $5$ vertices confirms that no choice gives more than $\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-26.title: Opposite pairs
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-26.body:
The numbers total $5050$ and form $50$ opposite pairs with a common sum, so each opposite pair sums to $101$. So the pairs are $\{x,101-x\}$ for $x=1,\dots,50$, each occupying opposite positions.

Count placements on a labelled circle of $100$ positions: choose which of the $50$ pairs goes at each of the $50$ position-pairs ($50!$ ways) and which element of each pair goes in the 'first' half ($2^{50}$ ways). Rotations are identified: divide by $100$. So the count is $\frac{50!\cdot2^{50}}{100}=49!\cdot2^{49}$.

**Answer: $49!\cdot2^{49}$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-27.title: Coordinates and similarity
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-27.body:
Take the regular tetrahedron with vertices $W=(1,0,0)$, $X=(0,1,0)$, $Y=(0,0,1)$, $Z=(1,1,1)$ (similar to $ABCD$), with centre $O=(\frac12,\frac12,\frac12)$. Gluing a congruent tetrahedron on face $XYZ$ puts the new vertex at the reflection $W'$ of $W$ in the plane $XYZ$; similarly for the others. For $Z$: the plane $x+y+z=1$ reflects $Z=(1,1,1)$ to $Z'=(-\frac13,-\frac13,-\frac13)$. Then $OZ'=\frac56\sqrt3$ while $OZ=\frac12\sqrt3$, so $W'X'Y'Z'$ is a scaled copy of $WXYZ$ with ratio $\frac{5/6}{1/2}=\frac53$. Volumes scale by $\left(\frac53\right)^3=\frac{125}{27}$, so $A'B'C'D'$ has volume $\frac{125}{27}$.

**Answer: $\frac{125}{27}$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-28.title: Blocks of men and women
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-28.body:
Look at maximal blocks of consecutive men and of consecutive women around the table. Every block has at least $2$ people (a lone man between two women would sit next to two women, one of whom is not his wife, which is not allowed -- and symmetrically for a lone woman). Where a block of men meets a block of women, the man and woman at the junction must be married, and each person has at most one such junction partner. Cases by number of blocks of each kind:

- **One block of each:** choose the $6$ seats of the men consecutively ($12$ ways), arrange the men ($6!$), the two women next to the ends of the block are determined, the other $4$ women are arranged in $4!$ ways: $6!\cdot12\cdot24=6!\cdot288$.
- **Two blocks of each:** block sizes $(a,b,c,d)$ with $a+c=b+d=6$ and all $\ge2$. Up to rotation there are $5$ patterns $[2,2,4,4],[2,3,4,3],[2,4,4,2],[3,2,3,4],[3,3,3,3]$, giving $12,12,12,12,6$ rotations respectively. In each, the men can be arranged in $6!$ ways, four of the women are forced (they touch a man) and the other two can be arranged in $2$ ways: $6!\cdot2\cdot(12+12+12+12+6)=6!\cdot108$.
- **Three blocks of each:** all blocks have size $2$: $4$ ways to choose the men's seats, $6!$ ways for the men, and the women are forced: $6!\cdot4$.

Total: $6!\,(288+108+4)=720\cdot400=288000$. A direct computer enumeration confirms $288000$.

**Answer: 288000**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-29.title: Divisibility condition
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-29.body:
For an integer polynomial, $b-2$ divides $f(b)-f(2)=8-2010=-2002$. So $b-2$ is a divisor (positive or negative) of $2002=2\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13$, which has $16$ positive divisors, so $32$ divisors in all. Conversely, for each such $b$ the linear polynomial $f(x)=\frac{2002}{2-b}(x-b)+8$ has integer coefficients and satisfies $f(b)=8$, $f(2)=2002+8=2010$. So there are $32$ values of $b$.

**Answer: 32**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-30.title: Reflect the target
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-30.body:
Place the hexagon with $A=(2,0)$, $B=(1,\sqrt3)$, $C=(-1,\sqrt3)$, $D=(-2,0)$, $E=(-1,-\sqrt3)$. The midpoint of $DE$ is $M=(-\frac32,-\frac{\sqrt3}2)$. Reflecting $M$ in the line $BC$ ($y=\sqrt3$) gives $M'=(-\frac32,\frac{5\sqrt3}2)$. The beam travels from $A$ straight toward $M'$ and meets $BC$ at $G$. The line from $A=(2,0)$ to $M'$ has parameter $t=\frac{\sqrt3}{5\sqrt3/2}=\frac25$ at height $\sqrt3$, so $G=\left(2-\frac72\cdot\frac25,\sqrt3\right)=\left(\frac35,\sqrt3\right)$. Then $BG=1-\frac35=\frac25$.

**Answer: $\frac25$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-31.title: Lattice paths
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-31.body:
Suppose there are $k$ ziplines. Let $a_0,\dots,a_k$ be the gaps between consecutive zipline endpoints on the left building (with $a_0$ the number of floors below the first zipline and $a_k$ the number above the last one), and $b_0,\dots,b_k$ the same on the right. Associate the path from $(0,0)$ that goes $a_0$ right, $b_0$ up, $a_1$ right, $b_1$ up, and so on, ending at $(5,5)$. Each configuration gives exactly one lattice path from $(0,0)$ to $(5,5)$ with right/up steps and each path gives exactly one configuration. The number of paths is $\binom{10}5=252$.

**Answer: 252**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-32.title: Square formed by tangents
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-32.body:
Let $O_1,O_2$ be the centres, $X$ the midpoint of $PQ$. Then $O_1O_2\perp PQ$, $O_1X=\sqrt{15^2-12^2}=9$ and $O_2X=\sqrt{13^2-12^2}=5$, so $O_1O_2=14$. The tangent radii $O_1R\perp AR$ and $O_2S\perp AS$; with $\angle RAS=90^\circ$ the lines $O_1R$ and $O_2S$ meet at a point $Y$ such that $ARYS$ is a square of side $s=AR$.

Then $YO_1=s-15$ and $YO_2=s-13$, and $\angle O_1YO_2=90^\circ$, so $(s-15)^2+(s-13)^2=14^2$, i.e. $s^2-28s+99=0$, $s=14\pm\sqrt{97}$. Since $YO_1=s-15>0$ is needed, $s=14+\sqrt{97}$.

**Answer: $14+\sqrt{97}$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-33.title: Telescoping identity
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-33.body:
For $n>k\ge1$: $$\frac{k+1}{k}\left(\frac1{\binom{n-1}{k}}-\frac1{\binom nk}\right)=\frac1{\binom n{k+1}}.$$ (Check: the left side simplifies, using $\binom nk-\binom{n-1}k=\binom{n-1}{k-1}$, to $\frac{(k+1)!\,(n-k-1)!}{n!}=\frac{1}{\binom n{k+1}}$.) Take $k=2008$ and sum over $n=2009,2010,\dots$: the terms $\frac1{\binom{n-1}{2008}}-\frac1{\binom n{2008}}$ telescope, leaving $\frac1{\binom{2008}{2008}}=1$. So the sum is $\frac{2009}{2008}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2009}{2008}$**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-34.title: Estimation
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-34.body:
This is an estimation question about a search-engine count in 2009; the official answer was $S=422000$ hits. Your score would have been $\max(25-|\ln A-\ln S|,0)$ points, so an answer within a factor of $e$ of $S$ already earns points.

**Official answer: 422000**

hmmt-nov-2009-guts-35.title: Mersenne prime exponents
hmmt-nov-2009-guts-35.body:
The radical numbers are exactly the exponents of Mersenne primes: $2,3,5,7,13,17,19,31,61,89,107,127,521,607,1279,2203,2281,3217,4253,4423,\dots$ The $20$th is $4423$. (In the contest, answers close to $S$ earned partial credit.)

**Answer: 4423**
